extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students studying patent infringement and validity principles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether an accused product/practice infringes a patent and related rules on novelty, utility, combinations, and specification sufficiency. Focuses on tests of substantial identity, essential proportions, and when differences are merely colorable or substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material or substantial difference versus colorable difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the alleged infringer has 'added anything material, not covered by the plaintiff's patent, which could be considered as constituting a subject-matter distinct from that of the plaintiffs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court asks if the difference is real and substantial, not merely colorable. Example: defendants' use of a woven fabric saturated with rubber may be a colorable imitation if the principle and result are the same. If differences are merely circuitous modes of doing what the patentee claimed, they do not avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuitous mode can still infringe if it falls within the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's circuitous or different-seeming process may still infringe if it achieves the same result within the scope of the patentee's claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walton v. Potter example: producing a cloth with rubber layers by a circuitous process was held to fall within the plaintiff's claim because it produced the same elasticity next to the teeth. Courts look to substance over form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions or degrees as part of the essence of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specification specifies particular proportions or degrees as the mode of producing a particular effect, those proportions form part of the essence of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another uses the same ingredients in materially different proportions (and thus an essentially different mode of working), that may not infringe. Where proportions are claimed as essential, differing proportions that still produce beneficial effects may constitute a different subject-matter (Hill v. Thompson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight departures intended solely to evade are fraudulent
rubrics_metrics.description: A slight departure from the specification made for the purpose of evasion is a fraud on the patent and does not avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will examine whether departures are substantive or merely attempts to evade; evasive changes require finding fraud and can defeat the defendant's defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of substantial identity: same means or known mechanical equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine sameness under patent law, courts ask whether the accused thing uses the same means (or known mechanical equivalent) to achieve the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the means employed are not the same and are not known equivalents, the modes of operation are not the same for patent purposes. This is the central test when comparing devices or methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superior practical utility can show a different principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one thing is practically and substantially better than another and the improvement is not gained by known mechanical equivalents, it is not the same in principle under patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superior utility may be an important test of identity: an improved machine that contains the whole substance of the older one plus something materially different may still infringe, but if the improvement is achieved by different means, it may be non-infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent protects the claimed subject-matter; combination patents protect the combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent stands upon its subject-matter: where a patent is for a combination, the protection is for that combination (not for the separate parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using any one of the individual parts of a claimed combination, without using the combination itself, is not infringement of the combination patent. Courts will look to whether the combination itself is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents claiming several distinct improvements: use of one may infringe but historical novelty-rule caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent is for several distinct improvements (not a single combination) the use of any one of them will be an infringement; historically, however, earlier courts required each claimed improvement to be new or the whole patent might be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier doctrine held that if novelty of any one claimed improvement failed, the whole patent could be void because the consideration was entire. Later statutes moderated this, allowing valid portions to survive if truly the patentee's invention and distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent invalidity where patent claims include things not new or known to be useless
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be void (or voidable) if it includes as part of the claimed invention one or more elements that were not new, or were known by the patentee to be useless when enrolled, thereby misleading the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (and the statute of July 4, 1836 §15) recognize defence that patentee was not first inventor of a substantial part. Statutes later permit severing and upholding that portion truly invented by the patentee unless broad claims were made wilfully to defraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of utility of claimed parts can vitiate a patent if misrepresented
rubrics_metrics.description: If parts claimed as essential are subsequently found useless, the patent is voidable where the patentee knew them to be useless when claiming them as useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent as a whole is useful, but some parts are useless, the patent may remain valid absent false suggestion. Jury findings that invention is useful 'on the whole' generally sustain validity unless there is evidence of knowing misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in form or proportion that produces a new effect may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every change in form or proportion is a mere trivial change: if changing form/proportion produces a new effect, it may amount to a change of principle and be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Justice Marshall's formulation: the word 'simply' in 'simply changing form or proportion' is limiting — only mere changes without new effect are unpatentable. Examples: substitution producing new, advantageous result (Davis v. Palmer; Earle v. Sawyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be sufficiently definite about quantities/degrees when they are part of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When degrees or quantities (e.g., proportion, heat) are essential to producing the claimed effect, the specification should state them; insufficiency or uncertainty may vacate a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slight defects in specification can vacate a patent; courts have required the specification to show by what degree of heat or what proportions the effect is to be produced. Evidence that proportions are non-essential supports non-infringement when proportions were claimed as essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and jury finding must address substance and result, not isolated answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations of infringement/identity rest on the substance and result of evidence; inconsistent or isolated testimony must be viewed in its substance and overall effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether witness testimony proves an essentially different mode of working. A single witness's testimony may be sufficient or insufficient depending on whether it shows a substantive difference in practice and result (Forman evidence example).
